abstract: The functions of polysaccharides are governed by their structures, making sample purity essential for robust structure-activity studies. Polygalacturonic acid (PGA) is widely used as a reference hydrocolloid in bioactivity and materials science research. However, commercial PGA is frequently contaminated with co-purifying polysaccharides, which complicates structure-activity relationship studies. This study identifies a prevalent impurity in commercial PGA and reveals its previously unrecognized, dual role in governing both immunostimulatory activity and hydrogel properties. Using chromatographic methods combined with enzymatic strategies, we isolated two distinct impurities and further purified PGA (pPGA). The impurities were determined to be a free β-1,4-galactan (Galactan) and a rhamnogalacturonan I decorated with β-1,4-galactan side chains (RGI) by structural analyses via MS, NMR, methylation and oligosaccharide profiling. Among them, only the RGI—which naturally carries galactan side chains—triggered a significant immune response in RAW264.7 cells, activating MAPK signaling and increasing levels of NO, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α In contrast, neither the pPGA nor the other impurity, Galactan, showed any immunostimulatory activity. Critically, this bioactive RGI was also essential for material properties. Its removal from commercial PGA markedly weakened the Ca 2+ -crosslinked gels, leading to reductions in both storage (G′) and loss (G″) moduli and resulting in a fragile microstructure. In contrast, the removal of the Galactan did not significantly affect the properties of the hydrogel. Our findings demonstrate that a co-purifying RGI, not PGA itself, is the decisive factor for key biological and physical functionalities attributed to commercial PGA. This finding emphasizes the importance of using structurally defined polysaccharides standards for accurate mechanistic research and controlled biomaterial design.

title: Multi-scale structure and rheological properties of curdlan/gelatin composite gels: Correlating molecular interactions with gelation mechanisms
Multiscale structural and functional characterisation of phenolic-reduced rapeseed protein isolates: Effects of phenolic removal and drying methods
abstract: Rapeseed proteins remain underutilised compared with soy and pea proteins despite their high protein content and balanced amino acid composition, largely because phenolic compounds impair solubility, structural integrity, and techno-functional performance. This study investigated how phenolic reduction and drying method collectively influence the structural organisation and hydrocolloid-related functionality of rapeseed protein isolates from brown and yellow varieties. Proteins were extracted following ethanol-assisted phenolic reduction, alkaline extraction (pH 10), and isoelectric precipitation (pH 4.5), followed by freeze drying or spray drying. Phenolic contents were markedly reduced from ∼68 to 93 mg GAE g −1 in rapeseed meals to ∼0.55–7.64 mg GAE g −1 in the final isolates, while nitrogen solubility index increased from ∼34 to 37% to ∼80–89%, indicating enhanced hydration and dispersibility after disruption of protein–phenolic interactions. SDS-PAGE and SEC analyses confirmed preservation of cruciferin- and napin-like proteins, whereas FTIR and CD analyses showed that freeze drying preserved β-sheet-rich structures and conformational stability, while spray drying promoted conformational rearrangement and aggregation. Nano-DSC further demonstrated higher denaturation enthalpies and greater thermal reversibility in freeze-dried isolates. These structural modifications strongly influenced functionality. Freeze-dried proteins exhibited higher dispersibility (∼28–39%), water-holding capacity (∼3.2 g/g), emulsifying stability (∼62–76 min), and stable gel formation at 10% protein concentration, whereas spray-dried isolates showed reduced rehydration and failed to form self-supporting gels even at 15% concentration. Overall, the results establish clear structure–process–function relationships linking phenolic reduction and drying-induced structural modification with hydrocolloid functionality in rapeseed protein systems.

Could corona-plasma treatment impact the antioxidant activity of phenolic compounds incorporated into gelatin coating applied onto PLA commercial films?
abstract: This study explores the possible impacts of the corona treatment (cold plasma) on bioactivity of natural antioxidants incorporated into fish gelatin-based composite films applied to biodegradable PLA. Indeed, physical-chemical characterisations were also investigated to better understand the potential modifications induced by the corona. The main objective was to evaluate the compatibility of corona treatment with bioactive packaging, to confirm its possible use in production and applications of active materials. Five phenolic acids (gallic, caffeic, ferulic, cinnamic, and p-coumaric) were added to the gelatin and then applied to PLA films, some of which were subsequently treated with plasma. The samples were characterized at different scales to analyze their wettability, solubility, water absorption capacity, molecular interactions (FTIR), antioxidant activity (DPPH), and UV opacity. The main results show that corona treatment slightly modifies contact angles, reflecting surface changes, without major chemical alterations of the polymer network. Neither solubility nor water absorption capacity are significantly affected by plasma, indicating weak interactions between gelatin and antioxidants. FTIR analysis confirms the absence of new covalent bonds or structural degradation of the gelatin matrix. The antioxidant activity, measured by DPPH, remains stable after treatment, proving the resistance of phenolic compounds to reactive plasma species in wet conditions. Finally, the UV opacity of the films increases significantly thanks to the antioxidants coupled with the corona process, thus improving their potential for protecting food against oxidation without being affected by corona. These results demonstrate the feasibility of corona treatment for bioactive films without compromising their functional properties and bioactivity.

Modulation of the physicochemical and functional properties of pea and faba bean protein isolates by high-intensity ultrasound and enzymatic hydrolysis
abstract: This comparative study investigated the use of individual treatments and sequential application of high-intensity ultrasound followed by enzymatic hydrolysis to modulate the physicochemical and functional properties of pea and faba bean protein isolates. Enzymatic hydrolysis shifted the peptide profile toward lower-molecular-weight peptides, while ultrasound induced unfolding and disrupted aggregates. These treatments impacted the surface activity and solubility of both isolates. Hydrolysis significantly enhanced solubility of pea (67.9% vs. 8.9%) and faba bean (43.6% vs. 7.3%) proteins; ultrasound was more effective at improving solubility in faba bean protein (64.2% vs. 7.3%) than in pea (19.9% vs. 8.9%). Ultrasound and enzymatic hydrolysis altered emulsifying and foaming properties through different mechanisms in a source-dependent manner. Ultrasound enhanced emulsion stability to a greater extent than enzymatic hydrolysis (100% vs. 73.3% for pea; 100% vs. 50.2% for faba bean) and achieved the smallest droplet sizes (3.1 vs. 5.7 μm for pea; 2.5 vs. 5.0 μm for faba bean). Hydrolysis, as well as ultrasound coupled with enzymatic hydrolysis, produced finer but less stable foams, whereas ultrasound promoted coarser foams with slower collapse and greater stability, especially in pea protein systems. Overall, structural rearrangements induced by ultrasound and enzymatic hydrolysis directly influenced both proteins’ interfacial interactions, improving solubility and emulsion formation. Foaming behaviour was modulated in both proteins, with overall improvement in stability observed mainly for pea. These findings highlight that tailoring modification strategies according to intrinsic characteristics of each protein source is crucial for adjusting their functionality in plant-based formulations and improving performance for specific applications.

title: Hydrocolloid and sweetener assisted stabilization of sucrose-free egg-white foams: from foam properties transfer to angel food cake quality
Emulsion-templated walnut oil oleogels stabilized by Maillard reaction-treated common bean protein as a solid fat substitute in bakery products
abstract: ABSTRACT Oleogels are structured systems for creating three-dimensional networks from liquid oils, used as an alternative to solid fat to reduce trans and saturated fat content. The approach of obtaining oleogels via concentrated emulsions and high internal phase emulsions (HIPEs) allows for long-term stability and low surfactant requirements. The Maillard reaction between proteins and carbohydrates is considered as a reliable and economical modification method, providing steric stabilization against droplet coalescence. It was hypothesized that Maillard-modified bean proteins could contribute to the physical and oxidative stability of walnut oil-based oleogels through improved solubility and steric hindrance. An emulsion-based walnut oil oleogel system stabilized with Maillard reaction-treated bean protein was developed for the first time. The degree of glycation, emulsion properties, and gelation capacity of the Maillard conjugates were investigated. This was followed by characterization of the emulsions and oleogels obtained with these conjugates (e.g., FTIR, GC-MS, oxidative stability). The oleogel with optimal properties was used as a margarine substitute in cookie formulations. Results indicated that the Maillard reaction-treated bean protein conjugate (MLC) exhibited high emulsion stability (ESI: 201.52 min) and low gelation concentration (5%). Moreover, the lowest oil loss (21.3%) and high thermal stability was achieved in the 30:70 (v/v) oleogel (OL) formulation. The presence of MLC in the oleogel structure improved the oxidative stability by decreasing the TBARS value from 0.33 to 0.26 mg MDA/g oil and K 232 values from 0.373 to 0.205 after 40 days of storage at room temperature. In cookie applications, the oleogel-based formulations provided hardness values between 39.5 and 69.9 N, compared to the control (38.2 N ± 2.6). These results indicated that MLC-based emulsion-templated oleogels can be used as a healthy solid fat replacement by preserving the high PUFA content of the oil.

Acheta domesticus protein extract as functional ingredient: physicochemical, thermal and rheological properties
abstract: This study investigates the techno-functional, thermal, and rheological properties of a protein extract obtained from defatted Acheta domesticus flour via thermally aided alkaline extraction coupled with isoelectric precipitation, aiming to evaluate its potential in diverse food applications. The resulting cricket protein extract (CPE) exhibited high protein content (85.65 %), and a marked pH-dependent solubility profile over the pH range 3–10, with a minimum near pH 4 and a value of 59.69 % at neutral pH. The extract also displayed favourable techno-functional properties, reaching a foaming capacity of 170 % and a foam stability of 92.59 % at pH 7. Emulsifying behaviour was likewise pH-dependent, with high emulsion stability maintained across the investigated pH range. Differential scanning calorimetry revealed a single endothermic denaturation peak near 55 °C (ΔH = 2.01 J g -1 ), indicating moderate thermal stability and suggesting the retention of organized protein domains. Rheological analysis showed concentration-dependent shear-thinning behaviour (n < 1) and weak-gel viscoelasticity after thermal treatment, with G′ higher than G″ and tan δ < 0.3. Network strength increased with concentration, indicating the ability of the extract to develop structured systems under processing-relevant conditions. Collectively, these findings indicate that A. domesticus protein extract is a functional, thermally responsive ingredient, showing performance within ranges reported for plant-based proteins and potential for use in food systems requiring water binding, interfacial stabilization, and elastic response, including meat analogue and related protein-based products.

Heat-induced changes in secondary structure, gelation and viscoelastic properties of potato protein and precision fermentation-derived β-lactoglobulin
abstract: This study investigates the influence of pH and protein blending on the denaturation, secondary structure transitions, gelation, and rheological properties of heat-set gels formed from patatin rich potato protein isolate (PPI) and precision fermentation-derived β-lactoglobulin (BLG). Using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and rheological analysis, we demonstrate that heat-induced gelation in both PPI and BLG is associated with the formation of intermolecular β-sheets and β-turns. PPI and BLG blends (PPI/BLG) show two distinct gelation pathways: At pH 4.5, non-interactive denaturation and gelation of the protein fractions occur, resulting in a firm but brittle gel dominated by PPI, with limited strain stiffening and energy dissipation onset. In contrast, at pH 6.0, interactive denaturation and network formation are observed. This is accompanied by a minor increase in β-turns, likely from the PPI fraction, which facilitates the formation of intermolecular β-sheets between PPI and BLG. Confocal microscopy indicated that this interaction leads to an interconnected dual network gel structure, exhibiting enhanced gel firmness, pronounced strain stiffening, and delayed energy dissipation. The rheological behavior of these dual network gels is dominated by BLG at low strains and by PPI at high strains, indicating effective stress-sharing between the networks. These findings highlight the potential of PPI/BLG blends to generate heat-set gels with tuneable texture and mechanical properties, inspiring their application as alternatives to animal-derived proteins in various food systems.

title: Structure-property relationships of pectin-alginate hydrocolloid films incorporated with B-phycoerythrin for pH-responsive functionality
abstract: The development of pH-sensitive hydrocolloid films represents a significant advance in intelligent food packaging, enabling visual monitoring of freshness and spoilage. In this study, pectin-alginate composite films incorporating B-phycoerythrin (B-PE, 38 μg/mL) were developed to investigate structure-property relationships and pH-responsive behavior. B-PE incorporation significantly modified the physicochemical properties of the films, reducing moisture content from 18.70 ± 0.16% to 14.01 ± 2.13% and decreasing the swelling index from 85% to 64%, while also lowering water solubility. Film thickness slightly increased from 0.277 to 0.282 mm, accompanied by statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05) in tensile strength and elongation at break, indicating reinforcement of the hydrocolloid network. The films exhibited antioxidant activity and antibacterial effects against Escherichia coli , Salmonella enterica , Listeria monocytogenes and Micrococcus luteus . A distinct color transition from purple to yellow was observed across a wide pH range (1–14), and the films detected ammonia concentrations between 0.125 and 1 mg/mL. Complete biodegradation (100%) was achieved after 10 days under soil burial conditions. These findings demonstrate that B-phycoerythrin functions as a multifunctional bioactive component, enhancing structural integrity while imparting pH-responsive sensing capability to pectin-alginate hydrocolloid films.

Surface hydrophobicity in protein–polysaccharide conjugates: A critical review of analytical methods, structural determinants, and implications for emulsification and foaming
abstract: Protein–polysaccharide conjugates have attracted increasing interest as functional hydrocolloid ingredients because they can modulate protein structure, interfacial behavior, and colloidal stability in complex food systems. Among the structural parameters commonly reported for these conjugates, surface hydrophobicity is one of the most frequently measured, yet its interpretation remains inconsistent across studies. This review examines surface hydrophobicity as a system-dependent parameter in protein–polysaccharide conjugates, with emphasis on its analytical determination, particularly by the widely used ANS (8-anilinonaphthalene-1-sulfonic acid) fluorescence method, and on the principal limitations of current approaches. Key factors affecting measured surface hydrophobicity are discussed, including protein source, polysaccharide type and structure, conjugation route, protein-to-polysaccharide ratio, pH, and ionic strength. The review also evaluates the relationship of surface hydrophobicity with hydrocolloid functionality, especially emulsification and foaming. Available evidence shows that increased surface hydrophobicity does not necessarily result in improved functional performance, because hydration, steric stabilization, solubility, and aggregation state also strongly influence interfacial behavior. Overall, this review highlights the need for more rigorous interpretation and standardized reporting of surface hydrophobicity in food hydrocolloid conjugates.

Designing wet-spun cultivated meat muscle fibers: The impact of faba bean protein isolate hydrolysis and concentration in a calcium-alginate system
abstract: ABSTRACT Replicating whole-muscle texture remains a central barrier for alternative proteins, with persistent gaps in soft-texture, fibrous anisotropy and moisture retention. Wet spinning offers a non-thermal, scalable route to produce aligned fibers, while enzymatic hydrolysis can tune protein physicochemical attributes to expand formulation options. This study evaluated faba bean protein isolate (FPI) at varied degrees of hydrolysis (DH 0-7.6%) and concentrations (0-6% w/w) as functional components in wet-spun calcium-alginate fibers designed for muscle mimetic analogs. Native and hydrolyzed FPI were characterized by SDS-PAGE and formol titration. Protein-alginate dispersions were assessed by confocal microscopy, ζ-potential, and rheological testing. Fibers were evaluated for morphology (SEM), cross-sectional area (CSA), Young's modulus, water-holding capacity (WHC), thermal stability (TGA), and early-stage ovine preadipocyte attachment. Hydrolysis shifted molecular weight from ∼18–100 kDa to <15 kDa and yielded dispersions with lower viscosity. Native FPI fibers (4-6% w/w) exhibited higher WHC (∼73% compared to ∼55%), elevated thermal degradation temperatures (∼295-310 °C compared to ∼242-256 °C), and significantly greater preadipocyte attachment than hydrolysate or control fibers. However, native FPI at high inclusion reduced Young's modulus (∼12 kPa) relative to hydrolysate formulations (∼20-23 kPa), potentially consistent with less uniform calcium-alginate network formation. Hydrolysate fibers maintained smooth, uniform morphology resembling alginate control. Protein physicochemical state, including native structure and degree of hydrolysis, functions as a primary design lever governing trade-offs between cell compatibility and matrix mechanics in wet-spun alginate-protein composites. These findings advance scaffold design for cultivated meat by establishing tunable protein parameters for balancing texture and cellular adhesion.

title: Improving heat stability and foam stability using mesoscale whey protein aggregates manufactured through an antisolvent-based method
abstract: This study investigated the physicochemical, interfacial, foaming and emulsifying properties of mesoscale whey protein aggregates (mWPA) produced through a scalable method involving liquid antisolvent (LAS) precipitation, heat treatment and microfluidization. These properties of mWPA were compared with two types control samples (1) untreated whey protein isolate (WPI) and (2) conventional whey protein aggregates (cWPA) induced by heat treatment. The mWPA exhibited more compact, spherical morphologies with particle size of ∼197 nm. These are distinct from cWPA and WPI, in which the former possessed a more fractal morphology with a smaller mean particle size (∼70 nm); while the latter had a spherical morphology but its mean particle size was significantly smaller. Physicochemical characterizations demonstrated that mWPA possessed higher surface hydrophobicity, higher surface charge, and improved colloidal stability after heating at 90 °C for 30 min compared to WPI. mWPA showed initial adsorption kinetics comparable to WPI at low protein concentrations ( 0.025-0.25%, wt/vol), but a lower equilibrium surface pressure at a high (1%, wt/vol), as revealed by dynamic adsorption measurements. This suggests restricted interfacial rearrangement and limited continuous adsorption for mWPA at the air-water interface. The foaming capacity of mWPA is comparable to WPI and cWPA, but it showed a superior foam stability, which was attributed to (1) stiffer interfacial films formed at lower (0.025%-0.05%, wt/vol) as evidenced by higher values obtained in dilatational rheology experiments, and (2) physical entrapment of particles within lamellae and Plateau borders at a higher (1%, wt/vol). In oil-in-water model emulsions, mWPA exhibited higher emulsifying activity than WPI but led to pronounced droplet flocculation and reduced emulsion stability with persistent flocculation, progressive coalescence and creaming during ambient storage. This study successfully demonstrated a scalable and distinctive method for modifying WPI, resulting in a protein colloidal particle with enhanced heat and foam stability.

Modeling the breakdown of starch gels during simulated mastication: role of salivary amylase, botanical origin, and retrogradation
abstract: ABSTRACT During oral processing, food structure changes are influenced by the mechanical forces of chewing and the enzymatic activity of salivary α-amylase (SA). This study explores the influence of SA on the textural and rheological properties of starch gels derived from corn, potato, and pea, stored for 0, 24, and 48 hours. Gels were subjected to repeated compression cycles and rheological testing, with and without saliva. Two models, first-order kinetics and Peleg’s model, were applied to describe the mechanical behavior under simulated mastication, and SEM analysis provided insights into the microstructure. Pea starch gels exhibited the highest hardness and G′, while potato gels were most susceptible to enzymatic hydrolysis. Storage promoted retrogradation, particularly in pea and potato starches, increasing rigidity. The fragile structure of potato gels against continuous mechanical compression facilitated the enzymatic action, notably reducing their gel integrity. Strong correlations were found between amylose content and resistant starch (r= 0.76; p <0.05), hardness parameters H inf (r=0.78, p <0.05) and Ho (r=0.86, p <0.05), as well as negative correlations with Peleg constants k 1 (r=-0.76, p <0.05) and k 2 (r=-0.77, p <0.05). Resistant starch also positively correlated with H inf (r = 0.80, p < 0.05) and Ho (r = 0.84, p < 0.05) and negatively correlated with k 2 (r = -0.79, p < 0.05), indicating that high amylose content promotes resistant starch formation and a hard, brittle gel network. Peleg’s model provided a better fit for textural changes during repeated compression and the saliva effect (R 2 = 82.76–94.43%) compared with the Box–Lucas model (R 2 = 35.18–91.10%). These findings reveal how enzymatic activity during oral processing affects the structure and function of starch gels.

title: Ultra-small-angle neutron scattering as a structural fingerprinting tool for commercial cheeses
abstract: Ultra-small-angle neutron scattering (USANS) was evaluated as a structural fingerprinting tool for the comparative characterization of commercial cheeses over length scales extending into the micrometer regime. Representative cheeses spanning a broad range of compositions and manufacturing styles exhibited distinct low-q scattering profiles, which were analyzed using simplified diffuse-scattering expressions to extract apparent power-law slopes as shape-based structural descriptors. The apparent low-q power-law slope varied systematically among cheese types, ranging from approximately –1.6 for ricotta to –2.9 for brie, indicating substantial differences in the scale dependence of mesoscale structural heterogeneity. Within the present sample set, fresher and higher-moisture cheeses such as ricotta and mozzarella displayed the shallowest apparent exponents, consistent with more open and coarse heterogeneity over the measured range, whereas ripened and firmer cheeses generally exhibited steeper decays. A cheddar ripening series further revealed that while 12-month and 2-year cheddar were adequately described by single apparent scaling regimes, 6-month cheddar exhibited a crossover between two slopes, suggesting hierarchical mesoscale organization. These results demonstrate that USANS provides a sensitive, non-destructive means of distinguishing cheese classes through compact scattering descriptors derived from the low-q intensity decay. The findings support the use of apparent power-law behavior as a practical comparative fingerprint of cheese mesoscale structure.

Pickering emulsion stabilisation by potato protein microgels: effect of pH and subphase
abstract: The aim of this study was to understand the effect of pH and oil subphase when stabilising emulsions by plant protein-based microgels versus non-microgelled counterparts. Potato protein microgels (PoPM) were used to stabilise Pickering oil-in-water (O-W) emulsions at pH 3 and 7 and subphase of varying polarity - tetradecane and octanol and compared against conventional emulsions stabilised by non-microgelled potato protein (PoP). Confocal microscopy and static light scattering were used to monitor changes in droplet size and microstructure during storage, whilst interfacial shear rheology was used to assess the viscoelasticity of the adsorbed interfacial protein layers using various subphases. Despite the larger oil droplet sizes and lower interfacial viscoelasticity observed for octanol emulsions, systems stabilised by PoPM appeared more resilient to environmental variations irrespective of pH or subphase. This is most likely due to the ca. 4 x larger size of the adsorbed entities of PoPM, promoting steric hindrance and the higher mechanical strength of the adsorbed PoPM films. Strikingly PoP unfolding (confirmed via dynamic light scattering and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS)) facilitated similar aggregation of PoP to thermally cross-linked PoPM, with resultant emulsion stability behaviour of PoP-stabilised emulsions resembling PoPM-stabilised ones at pH 3. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding how using plant protein microgels may offer benefits to interfacial stabilisation when the polarity of subphase varies, such as stabilising essential oils versus vegetable oils, which has been relatively underexplored in the literature.

High moisture extrusion of fava bean protein blend: Evaluating potato protein as gluten replacement for texture enhancement
abstract: High-moisture extrusion (HME) enables fibrous structuring of plant proteins for meat analogues where wheat gluten (WG) remains a prevalent texture aid with allergenicity concerns. This study evaluated whether potato protein isolate (PPI) can be a gluten-free structuring agent for texturizing fava bean protein isolate (FPI) during HME. FPI, FPI–WG, and FPI–PPI blends (75:25 w/w) were extruded and assessed for functional properties, colour, texture, nonlinear rheology, protein–protein interactions, microstructure, and taste profiling. The PPI increased specific mechanical energy relative to FPI and WG and produced co-extrudates with the highest surface hydrophobicity (11,824) and strongest intrinsic fluorescence quenching (68.3a.u.), indicating extensive unfolding and aggregation. When co-extrudate with FPI, WG lowered hardness and increased springiness compared to PPI. Both co-extrudates E(FPI-WG) and E(FPI-PPI) increased disulfide-linked protein fractions (31–33%) relative to E(FPI) (21.8%), while E(FPI-PPI) exhibited the strongest nonlinear viscoelastic response. The study also elucidates the mechanistic underpinnings of gluten-free texturization in E(FPI-PPI) demonstrating hybrid protein–protein network formation by PPI primarily through covalent interactions. Oil-holding capacity of extrudate increased specifically with PPI (211.8%) compared to WG which is due to the combination of higher surface hydrophobicity and porous architecture of E(FPI-PPI). Overall, PPI formed a reinforced hybrid interaction network with FPI upon HME, supporting its viability as a gluten-free structuring agent for fava-based meat analogues. However, e-tongue based taste profiling revealed stronger bitterness and astringency with prolonged aftertastes in E(FPI-PPI) which underscores a formulation trade-off as PPI enhances network strength but necessitates bitterness mitigation strategies compared to WG.

Characterization and structural analysis of egg yolk plasma
abstract: Egg yolk plasma is the main contributor to the emulsifying and gelling properties of egg yolk. Despite its functional importance, and although extensive physicochemical studies have been conducted, further in-depth characterization of its colloidal components, namely the low-density lipoproteins (LDLs), is needed. In this study, egg yolk plasma was prepared at two ionic strengths (0.1 and 0.2 M NaCl) and centrifuged at 10,000 or 40,000 × g to investigate the influence of extraction conditions on composition, structure, and functionality. Increasing NaCl reduced plasma lipid content and increased the relative abundance of LDL apoproteins. Increasing centrifugal force increased the proportion of neutral lipids and decreased the proportion of polar lipids. Despite these compositional differences, dynamic light scattering and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) consistently showed a dominant LDL population centered at 40-50 nm across all conditions, indicating structural robustness. The SAXS data were successfully described using a core-shell model, supporting a low-electron-density lipid core surrounded by a protein- and phospholipid-rich shell, with dimensions consistent across treatments. Temperature-dependent SAXS showed that LDL particles remained structurally stable up to ∼65 °C, above which they showed increased interparticle aggregation, followed by pronounced anisotropy and restructuring above ∼70 °C. Plasma prepared at 40,000 × g formed the stiffest heat-induced gels, whereas plasma prepared at 10,000 × g reached lower equilibrium interfacial tension and higher interfacial viscoelastic moduli at equal protein concentration. Overall, moderate variations in extraction conditions did not alter LDL structure but induced compositional changes that modulated interparticle interactions and functionality, supporting the view of egg yolk plasma as a structurally robust yet functionally tunable colloidal system.
